parts.name: Arrival
parts.stand: On the waterfront, facing out across the water toward the lighthouse at the harbor mouth.

paras.t: Here it is: the old harbor of Chania. The old town grew up right behind you, around this water, and the whole city spread out from here. And out at the harbor entrance, that stone tower is the lighthouse.
Mind the edge of the quay as you walk. There's not much shade by the water, so keep a hat and some water handy.

One travel guide puts it well. It calls the old town a maze of alleys and houses that stood for hundreds of years, were rebuilt, ruined, and rebuilt again, with details from different epochs. Keep that in mind as you look along this waterfront. Hardly anything here belongs to just one century.
The quays have their own names: Akti Tompazi, Akti Kountouriotou, and Akti Enoseos, which is the marina. All of them have historical buildings, and all of them have nightlife.

parts.name: The lighthouse
parts.stand: Keep facing the lighthouse at the harbor entrance.

paras.t: The lighthouse you're looking at was rebuilt in the nineteenth century, on the base of an older Venetian one. That base is all that's left of the first lighthouse. It's a stone tower, rising 26 meters, about 85 feet, above the bay.

So who built the tower you see? Not the Venetians. Under Venice, this spot was a naval post, there to protect the city from oncoming Turks or pirates. In 1645 the Turks took the city, and the old lighthouse was left to fall into ruin. The rebuilding, in the nineteenth century, is credited to Egyptian troops who were helping the Ottoman Empire hold Crete.

It's had an eventful life since. In May 1915 it got a fixed white light, and became an official lighthouse in Greece's network. It was damaged in World War Two, and refurbished in 2006. Today the light at the top flashes red every 2.5 seconds. If you're here after dark, try counting along. And since 1962, the tower has been a listed archaeological site.

parts.name: Who sailed from here
parts.stand: Turn around and look back along the waterfront, toward the town.

paras.t: This harbor is far older than Venice. The small hill right next to the seafront is Kastelli, the harbor's citadel. Digs there have turned up finds from the Neolithic all the way through the Minoan age.

In the late Minoan age, the town here, ancient Kydonia, was a large commercial and maritime center. It exported pottery, oil, perfume and wine across the Aegean. In 2025, UNESCO listed ancient Kydonia as a World Heritage Site, one of six Minoan palatial centers on that list.
The Odyssey even mentions a people called the Cydonians. Their city was important enough for that.

How did Venice get Crete at all? After the Fourth Crusade in 1204, the island went to Bonifacio, Marquess of Montferrat, and he sold it to the Venetians for 1000 silver marks. Historians estimate that about 10,000 Venetians moved to Crete in the first century, at a time when Venice itself had around 60,000 people. The cultures mixed closely, but the Cretans kept their Greek Orthodox faith.

Then came Venice. In 1252, Venetian settlers founded Canea, today's Chania, on the site of long-abandoned Kydonia. They strengthened its defenses and gave the town the shape it still has. Over on the west side of the harbor is the Firkas Fortress, built early in the seventeenth century to protect it.

After the Ottomans took the city, they built new mosques, among them the Küçük Hasan Pasha Mosque, also called the Yali Mosque, on the harbor. I'll be honest with you: beyond that, my sources say very little about it, so I won't guess at its story.
In Ottoman times, the pasha of Crete resided here, in Hanya, as they called the town.

parts.name: Before you go
parts.stand: Wherever you like along the water.

paras.t: Minoan traders, Venetian sailors, Ottoman troops, Egyptian builders. They all looked out at this same water. Take a moment before you go. This harbor has been the town's front door for a very long time, and right now, it's yours.
In the 1970s, Crete became a major destination for travelers. You're part of that story now.
